chapters.title: Networking I: TCP/IP, TLS & DNS
chapters.blurb: How bytes actually get from one machine to another: IP routing, TCP reliability and congestion control, the TLS 1.3 handshake, and DNS resolution. The layer under every distributed-systems answer.

b: Practical stack: link (Ethernet/Wi‑Fi frames, MAC addresses), network (IP packets, routing), transport (TCP/UDP, ports), application (HTTP, DNS, TLS on top of TCP).
Each layer encapsulates the one above: an HTTP request sits inside TLS records, inside TCP segments, inside IP packets, inside Ethernet frames.
A connection is identified by the 5‑tuple: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port.
L4 devices (NAT, L4 load balancers, firewalls) see IPs and ports; L7 devices (reverse proxies, API gateways) parse HTTP and need to terminate TLS.
Interview shortcut: when debugging, ask which layer broke — DNS (name), IP (route), TCP (connect/reset/timeout), TLS (cert/handshake), or HTTP (status code).
IP is best‑effort: packets can be dropped, duplicated, reordered or delayed. Reliability is the transport layer's job.
Routers forward by longest‑prefix match on the destination address against their routing table; CIDR like 10.0.0.0/16 means the first 16 bits are the network.
Between organisations, BGP exchanges reachability for prefixes; inside a cloud VNet/VPC, the provider's software‑defined routing does the work.
MTU (often 1500 bytes on Ethernet) limits packet size. Path MTU problems show up as connections that handshake fine but hang on large transfers.
TTL (hop limit) is decremented at each router so looping packets die; traceroute exploits this to discover hops.
Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are not routable on the internet and need NAT to reach out.
Three‑way handshake: client SYN (with initial sequence number), server SYN‑ACK, client ACK. Costs one round trip before data can flow.
Options are negotiated in the SYN: MSS, window scaling, SACK, timestamps.
The server keeps half‑open connections in a SYN queue and completed ones in an accept queue; if the app doesn't accept() fast enough, the accept queue overflows and new connections are dropped.
Teardown is per direction: FIN/ACK each way (often four segments). A RST aborts immediately — e.g. connecting to a closed port or a peer that crashed.
SYN floods fill the SYN queue; SYN cookies let the server avoid storing state until the final ACK arrives.
Every byte has a sequence number; the receiver sends cumulative ACKs for the next byte it expects. SACK lets it report non‑contiguous blocks received.
Retransmission timeout (RTO) is computed from smoothed RTT plus variance, with exponential backoff on repeated losses — why a lost packet can cost hundreds of ms or seconds.
Fast retransmit: three duplicate ACKs signal a likely loss, so the sender retransmits without waiting for RTO.
A lost SYN uses an initial RTO (commonly around 1 second) — one dropped SYN visibly adds ~1s to connection setup.
TCP gives an ordered, reliable byte stream with no message boundaries — applications must frame messages themselves (length prefixes, delimiters, HTTP framing).
Flow control protects the receiver: the receive window (rwnd) advertises how much buffer space is free. A slow reader shrinks it to zero and the sender stalls.
Congestion control protects the network: the sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd) and sends at most min(cwnd, rwnd) unacknowledged bytes.

Slow start grows cwnd exponentially from a small initial window until loss or a threshold; then congestion avoidance grows it roughly linearly (AIMD: additive increase, multiplicative decrease on loss).
Algorithms: Reno/CUBIC are loss‑based; BBR models bottleneck bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting only to loss.
Throughput ceiling ≈ window / RTT. The bandwidth‑delay product tells you how big buffers/windows must be to fill a long fat pipe.
New connections start slow, which is why connection reuse and pooling matter so much for latency.
Nagle's algorithm holds back small segments while earlier data is unacknowledged, coalescing tiny writes into fewer packets.
Delayed ACK makes the receiver wait briefly (tens of ms up to ~200ms depending on OS) hoping to piggyback the ACK on response data.
Together they can stall: the sender waits for an ACK before sending the rest; the receiver waits for more data before ACKing — classic 40–200ms latency spikes on write‑write‑read patterns.
Fix: set TCP_NODELAY on latency‑sensitive sockets (most RPC frameworks and database drivers do), or build each message in one buffer and write once.
TCP_CORK / MSG_MORE are the opposite: deliberately batch until you uncork.
The side that closes first enters TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL (60s on Linux) so stray delayed segments don't corrupt a new connection with the same 5‑tuple and the final ACK can be resent.
A client opening many short connections to the same destination can exhaust ephemeral ports (each 5‑tuple stuck in TIME_WAIT).
Fixes: connection pooling/keep‑alive (best), widening the ephemeral port range, more source IPs, or tcp_tw_reuse for outgoing connections. Avoid the long‑removed tcp_tw_recycle.
In the cloud, SNAT port exhaustion on a NAT gateway or load balancer is the same problem one level up — a frequent Azure outbound‑connectivity issue.
CLOSE_WAIT piling up means your application received FIN but never closed the socket — an app bug (leaked connections), not a kernel tuning issue.
TCP delivers bytes in order: one lost segment stalls everything behind it, even data for unrelated logical streams. That is transport‑level head‑of‑line blocking.
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, so a single loss blocks all streams; QUIC (HTTP/3) runs over UDP and does loss recovery per stream.
UDP: connectionless datagrams, no handshake, no ordering, no retransmits, no congestion control. Message boundaries are preserved.
Used where latency beats reliability or the app does its own reliability: DNS queries, VoIP/video, gaming, QUIC, metrics (StatsD).
Apps on UDP must handle loss, reordering, duplication, and should implement their own congestion control to be good network citizens.
Goals: confidentiality (encryption), integrity (AEAD ciphers), and authentication of the server (and optionally client) via certificates.
TLS 1.3 is 1‑RTT: ClientHello carries supported ciphers plus a key share (ephemeral (EC)DHE); ServerHello replies with its key share, then encrypted certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished.
Ephemeral Diffie–Hellman gives forward secrecy: stealing the server's private key later doesn't decrypt past recorded traffic.
Resumption with a pre‑shared key can allow 0‑RTT early data — but 0‑RTT data is replayable, so only use it for idempotent requests.
Total cold cost over TCP: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS 1.3) before the first request byte; TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTTs for the handshake.
SNI in the ClientHello names the host so one IP can serve many certificates; ALPN negotiates the application protocol (h2, http/1.1).
A certificate binds a public key to names (SANs) and is signed by a CA. The client validates the chain up to a trusted root, checks hostname match, validity dates, and possibly revocation (OCSP/CRL).
Servers must send intermediates; a missing intermediate is a classic "works in browser, fails in curl/Java" bug because browsers may cache or fetch intermediates.
Cert expiry is a top cause of outages — automate rotation (ACME, Key Vault/cert‑manager) and alert well before expiry.
mTLS: the server also requests a client certificate, giving strong service‑to‑service identity. Common in service meshes and zero‑trust networks.
TLS termination at a load balancer simplifies certs but means traffic behind it is plaintext unless you re‑encrypt to the backend.
Stub resolver (in the OS) asks a recursive resolver; on a miss, the recursive walks root → TLD (.com) → authoritative servers, then caches the answer.
Records: A/AAAA (addresses), CNAME (alias), MX, TXT, NS, SRV. A CNAME can't coexist with other records at the same name, so apex domains use ALIAS/flattening features.
Every answer has a TTL; caches (resolvers, OS, language runtimes, connection pools) may hold it that long — or longer if they misbehave. Negative answers are cached too.
Low TTLs speed failover but increase query load and latency; lower TTLs before a planned migration, not during the incident.
DNS mostly uses UDP port 53 with TCP fallback for large responses; DNS failures look like "everything is down" because nothing can find anything.
Anycast: many sites announce the same IP prefix via BGP; the network routes each client to the "nearest" site in routing terms.
Used for DNS root/resolvers, CDNs, DDoS absorption and global front doors (e.g. Azure Front Door, Cloudflare).
Works best for short or stateless exchanges; long TCP connections can break if routing shifts mid‑flow to another site.
Contrast with DNS‑based geo load balancing (Azure Traffic Manager style): different IPs handed out per client region, limited by TTL caching and resolver location.
Failover with anycast is fast: withdraw the route from the unhealthy site and traffic shifts without waiting for DNS TTLs.

qs.q: Which identifies a single TCP connection?
o: The 5‑tuple: protocol, source IP/port, destination IP/port
qs.e: Many clients can hit the same server port; the source side differentiates them.

qs.q: How many round trips does the TCP handshake cost before the client can send data (without TCP Fast Open)?
qs.e: SYN, SYN‑ACK, ACK: one RTT; the client can send data with its ACK.

qs.q: What does IP guarantee about delivery?
o: Nothing: best effort, packets may be lost, duplicated or reordered
qs.e: Reliability is added by TCP or the application.

qs.q: Flow control in TCP primarily protects…
o: The receiver from being overwhelmed, via the advertised receive window
qs.e: rwnd reflects free receive buffer space.

qs.q: Congestion control limits in‑flight data using…
o: The congestion window (cwnd), combined with rwnd as min(cwnd, rwnd)
qs.e: The sender estimates what the network path can carry.

qs.q: What triggers TCP fast retransmit?
qs.e: Duplicate ACKs suggest a hole; retransmit without waiting for RTO.

qs.q: Why can one dropped SYN add about a second to connection setup?
o: The initial retransmission timeout is conservative (commonly ~1s) since there is no RTT sample yet
qs.e: No RTT estimate exists yet, so the first RTO is large.

qs.q: Throughput of a single TCP flow is roughly bounded by…
qs.e: You can only have one window of unacked data per round trip.

qs.q: A client writes a 10‑byte header and then a 200‑byte body in two writes, then waits for a reply, and sees ~40ms stalls. Likely cause?
o: Nagle's algorithm interacting with delayed ACK
qs.e: Set TCP_NODELAY or write the message in one call.

qs.q: Which side of a TCP connection enters TIME_WAIT?
o: The side that actively closes first
qs.e: The active closer holds TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL.

qs.q: Lots of sockets stuck in CLOSE_WAIT on your service usually means…
o: The application received the peer's FIN but never closed its socket
The peer has not sent FIN
qs.e: CLOSE_WAIT is waiting on the local app to close — a leak.

qs.q: Best fix for ephemeral port exhaustion from many short outbound HTTP calls?
qs.e: Fewer new connections means fewer TIME_WAIT 5‑tuples.

qs.q: Why does HTTP/2 over TCP still suffer head‑of‑line blocking?
o: It uses one stream per connection
A lost TCP segment stalls the whole in‑order byte stream, blocking all multiplexed streams
qs.e: Multiplexing is above TCP, which knows nothing of streams.

qs.q: Which is true of UDP?
o: It preserves message boundaries but provides no reliability or congestion control
qs.e: Datagrams are independent; loss handling is up to the app.

qs.q: How many round trips does a full TLS 1.3 handshake add on top of TCP?
qs.e: TLS 1.3 sends key shares in the first flight; TLS 1.2 needed two.

qs.q: What provides forward secrecy in TLS 1.3?
qs.e: Session keys can't be recovered from the long‑term key later.

qs.q: Why is TLS 1.3 0‑RTT early data risky?
o: It can be replayed by an attacker, so it should only carry idempotent requests
qs.e: Early data lacks the fresh server input that protects against replay.

qs.q: What does SNI do?
o: Tells the server which hostname the client wants, so it can pick the right certificate
qs.e: Lets many TLS sites share one IP. ALPN negotiates h2.

qs.q: A service works in browsers but Java clients fail with "unable to find valid certification path". Most likely?
o: The server is not sending the intermediate certificate
qs.e: Browsers often fill gaps; strict clients need the full chain.

qs.q: What does mTLS add over normal TLS?
o: The client also presents a certificate, so the server authenticates the client
qs.e: Mutual authentication for service‑to‑service identity.

qs.q: In recursive DNS resolution, who walks root → TLD → authoritative?
o: The stub resolver in the OS
qs.e: Stub asks recursive; recursive does the walk and caches.

qs.q: You plan to move a service to new IPs. What should you do with DNS TTLs?
o: Lower them at the moment of the switch
Raise them right before the move
Lower them well in advance, wait out the old TTL, then switch
qs.e: Caches keep the old record until the old TTL expires.

qs.q: Why can't you put a CNAME at a zone apex like example.com?
o: A CNAME cannot coexist with other records, and the apex must have SOA/NS records
qs.e: Providers offer ALIAS/flattening as a workaround.

qs.q: What is anycast?
o: Sending one packet to all hosts
Multiple sites announcing the same IP prefix so routing delivers each client to a nearby one
qs.e: BGP picks the "closest" site.

qs.q: What does an overflowing accept queue look like to clients?
o: Connections dropped or timing out / retrying SYNs while the app isn't calling accept() fast enough
qs.e: Slow accept loops or a small backlog cause it.

qs.q: Clients in another region see 3s+ tail latency to your API; server traces show 20ms handling. Packet captures show occasional SYN retransmits. Best explanation and fix?
o: Loss on new connections hits large initial RTOs; reuse warm pooled connections and investigate the lossy path
TLS 1.3 is too slow; downgrade to 1.2
DNS TTLs are too long; lower them
qs.e: Handshake losses cost whole RTOs; warm connections avoid repeated handshakes and slow start.

qs.q: A service on Azure making many outbound calls to one third‑party API fails intermittently with connection timeouts at high load, while the API is healthy. Most likely culprit?
o: SNAT port exhaustion from opening a new connection per request
qs.e: Each new outbound flow consumes a SNAT port; pooling or a NAT gateway with more IPs fixes it.

qs.q: Large uploads hang mid‑transfer through a VPN, while small requests work fine. Most likely cause?
o: A path MTU problem (e.g. ICMP blocked so PMTU discovery fails), so full‑size packets are silently dropped
qs.e: Small packets fit; big ones vanish. Fix with MSS clamping or allowing ICMP.

qs.q: You cut over DNS to a new load balancer with TTL 60s, but some clients still hit the old one hours later. Why?
o: Clients or runtimes cache DNS beyond TTL (e.g. JVM settings) and long‑lived pooled connections never re‑resolve
qs.e: Keep the old endpoint alive and bound connection lifetime so clients re‑resolve.

qs.q: A transfer between two regions (100ms RTT) caps at ~5 MB/s despite a 1 Gbps link and no loss. What do you check first?
o: Window sizes: receive buffers / window scaling too small for the bandwidth‑delay product
qs.e: Throughput ≈ window/RTT: 512KB / 0.1s ≈ 5MB/s. Filling 1Gbps needs ~12.5MB in flight.

terms: Protocol + source/destination IP and port identifying a flow
Maximum TCP payload per segment, negotiated in SYN
Retransmission timeout derived from smoothed RTT and variance
Receive window: receiver's free buffer, for flow control
Congestion window: sender's estimate of what the path can carry
Exponential cwnd growth from a small initial window
Bandwidth × RTT: bytes in flight needed to fill a link
Coalesces small writes while data is unacknowledged
Active closer's 2×MSL wait to absorb stray segments
One lost/slow item stalls everything queued behind it
Past sessions stay safe if the long‑term key leaks
Hostname in ClientHello so the server picks the right cert
TLS extension negotiating the application protocol (h2, http/1.1)
Both sides present certificates for mutual authentication
Same IP announced from many sites; routing picks the nearest

drills.p: Explain everything that happens on the network before the first byte of an HTTPS request reaches the server, and how much latency each step costs.
a: DNS lookup (cached, or recursive walk costing several RTTs)
TCP three‑way handshake: 1 RTT
TLS 1.3 handshake: 1 RTT (2 for TLS 1.2), certificate validation
SNI and ALPN select cert and protocol
Slow start limits how fast the first response arrives
Connection reuse/pooling removes all of these for later requests

drills.p: Compare flow control and congestion control in TCP, and explain why new connections are slow.
a: Flow control: receiver advertises rwnd to avoid overflowing its buffer
Congestion control: sender's cwnd protects the network
Effective window = min(cwnd, rwnd)
Slow start then AIMD; loss‑based (CUBIC) vs model‑based (BBR)
Throughput ≈ window/RTT
New connections start with small cwnd, hence pooling and keep‑alive

drills.p: Your service shows thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT and some in CLOSE_WAIT. Explain what each means and what you would do.
a: TIME_WAIT: normal for the active closer, lasts 2×MSL
Only a problem when it exhausts ephemeral/SNAT ports
Fix with connection reuse, more ports/IPs, tcp_tw_reuse for outbound
CLOSE_WAIT: peer closed, local app never closed — a leak
Fix CLOSE_WAIT in code: close/dispose connections, check pool handling

chapters.title: Networking II: HTTP, load balancing & the edge
chapters.blurb: HTTP versions, API styles, load balancers, CDNs and proxies: the layer where most production latency, retries and outages actually live.

b: Text protocol: request line, headers, optional body. Persistent connections (keep‑alive) are the default in HTTP/1.1, avoiding a new TCP+TLS handshake per request.
Effectively one outstanding request per connection (pipelining is rarely used), so clients open several connections per host (browsers ~6).
Bodies are framed by Content‑Length or chunked transfer encoding; disagreement between proxies about which applies is the root of request‑smuggling attacks.
Idle keep‑alive connections are closed by whichever side has the shorter idle timeout — if the server closes just as the client reuses it, the client sees a reset on a "healthy" connection.
Rule: client idle timeout shorter than the server/LB idle timeout, and retry idempotent requests on stale‑connection errors.
Binary framing; many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, interleaved as frames. Removes the need for many connections per host.
HPACK header compression shrinks repetitive headers (cookies, auth tokens).
Flow control per stream and per connection; servers advertise max concurrent streams.
Still on TCP, so one packet loss stalls all streams (transport head‑of‑line blocking).
One long‑lived connection can defeat L4 load balancing: all of a client's requests stick to one backend. Use L7 balancing or cap connection age.
gRPC runs on HTTP/2, which is why it needs HTTP/2‑aware proxies end to end.
QUIC is a transport over UDP with TLS 1.3 built in: combined transport+crypto handshake in 1 RTT, 0‑RTT on resumption.
Streams are independent at the transport level, so a loss only blocks the affected stream.
Connection IDs instead of the 5‑tuple let connections survive client IP changes (Wi‑Fi to cellular).
Encrypted transport headers limit middlebox interference but make debugging and some network monitoring harder.
Downsides: UDP sometimes blocked or rate‑limited, more CPU in user space; clients fall back to HTTP/2. Discovered via Alt‑Svc headers or HTTPS DNS records.
Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) shouldn't change state. Idempotent methods (safe ones plus PUT, DELETE) have the same effect when repeated. POST and PATCH are not idempotent by default.
Retries are only automatically safe for idempotent requests; for POST use idempotency keys (Stripe‑style Idempotency‑Key header) stored server‑side with the result.
2xx success (201 Created, 204 No Content); 3xx redirects (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified).
4xx client errors: 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409 conflict, 422 validation, 429 rate limited (honour Retry‑After).
5xx server errors: 500 bug, 502 bad gateway (invalid response or reset from upstream), 503 unavailable/overloaded, 504 gateway timeout (upstream too slow).
Retry 429/503 with backoff and jitter; don't blindly retry other 4xx.
REST: resources + HTTP verbs, JSON, cacheable GETs, universal tooling, human‑readable. Great for public APIs (Stripe's API is REST).
gRPC: Protobuf schemas, HTTP/2, generated clients, streaming (unary, server, client, bidi), deadlines propagated. Great for internal service‑to‑service calls.
gRPC trade‑offs: needs HTTP/2 end to end, browsers need gRPC‑Web or a proxy, binary payloads are harder to debug.
GraphQL: client chooses fields from one endpoint; avoids over/under‑fetching but complicates caching, authorization and query‑cost limits.
Versioning: additive changes are safe; Protobuf field numbers must never be reused; public REST APIs often pin versions per client (Stripe uses dated versions).
WebSocket: HTTP Upgrade to a full‑duplex, message‑framed connection. Good for chat, collaboration, live dashboards.
Server‑Sent Events: one‑way server→client stream over plain HTTP, text events, automatic reconnect with Last‑Event‑ID. Simpler when the client only listens.
Long polling: client holds a request open until data arrives, then re‑requests. Works everywhere but costs a request per message batch.
Operational issues: long‑lived connections pin to one backend, complicate deploys (must drain/reconnect), and hit proxy idle timeouts — send heartbeats/pings.
Scaling needs a pub/sub backplane (Redis, Kafka, Azure SignalR/Web PubSub) so any node can deliver to any connected user.
L4 balances TCP/UDP flows by 5‑tuple; doesn't parse HTTP. Very fast, protocol agnostic, can pass TLS through untouched. Examples: Azure Load Balancer, AWS NLB.
L7 terminates HTTP(S) and routes per request: by path, host, header; can retry, rewrite, add auth, do canaries. Examples: Azure Application Gateway/Front Door, Envoy, NGINX, AWS ALB.
Algorithms: round robin, least connections/least outstanding requests, consistent hashing (sticky by key), power of two random choices.
L4 with long‑lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections leads to imbalance; L7 balances per request.
Client IP is lost behind proxies unless passed via X‑Forwarded‑For / Forwarded headers, or PROXY protocol at L4.
Active health checks probe an endpoint on an interval; passive checks (outlier detection) eject backends that error on live traffic.
Liveness ("restart me if I'm wedged") differs from readiness ("send me traffic now"). Don't make liveness depend on downstream services, or one DB blip restarts your whole fleet.
Readiness should fail during startup warm‑up and during shutdown so the LB stops sending new traffic.
Connection draining: on removal/deploy, stop new requests to the instance but let in‑flight ones finish within a deadline.
Graceful shutdown: fail readiness → wait for LB to notice → stop accepting → finish in‑flight → close idle keep‑alive connections → exit.
CDNs cache content at edge PoPs near users, cutting latency and origin load; they also terminate TLS close to the user and absorb DDoS.
Cache‑Control: max‑age (all caches), s‑maxage (shared caches only), public/private, no‑store (never store), no‑cache (store but revalidate before use).
Validators: ETag/If‑None‑Match and Last‑Modified/If‑Modified‑Since give cheap 304 Not Modified revalidations.
stale‑while‑revalidate and stale‑if‑error serve slightly old content while refreshing or when the origin is down.
Cache key matters: Vary headers, query strings and cookies can fragment the cache or leak personalised responses. Never cache authenticated responses as public.
Invalidate with versioned/fingerprinted URLs (app.3f9a.js) rather than relying on purges.
Every network call needs timeouts: a short connect timeout, a request/read timeout, and an overall deadline propagated through the call chain.
Retries multiply: 3 attempts at each of 4 layers = up to 3^4 = 81 calls at the bottom. Retry at one layer, with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget.
Deadlines should shrink as they go down the chain: an inner call shouldn't keep working after the outer caller has already given up.
Keep‑alive: align idle timeouts (client < LB < server), and cap connection lifetime so DNS changes and rebalancing take effect.
TCP keepalive (kernel probes, default idle ~2h on Linux) differs from HTTP keep‑alive (connection reuse); lower TCP keepalive to detect dead peers and keep NAT entries alive.
Forward proxy acts for clients (corporate egress, outbound filtering). Reverse proxy acts for servers (TLS termination, routing, caching, rate limiting).
Service mesh sidecars (Envoy) proxy every pod's traffic, adding mTLS, retries and telemetry without app changes — at the cost of extra hops and complexity.
NAT rewrites addresses/ports; SNAT lets many private hosts share public IPs by mapping to distinct source ports. NAT tables have idle timeouts.
A NAT/firewall silently dropping an idle flow looks like a hang on next use — fix with keepalives shorter than the idle timeout (Azure LB/NAT defaults are a few minutes).
API gateways are L7 reverse proxies adding auth, quotas, routing and request transformation.

cards.t: What happens when you type a URL
b: Browser parses the URL, checks HSTS and caches; DNS resolution (browser, OS, recursive resolver, authoritative), often landing on a CDN's anycast or geo‑DNS address.
TCP handshake (or QUIC), TLS handshake with SNI/ALPN, certificate validation.
HTTP request to edge/CDN; a cache hit returns immediately; a miss goes to origin via load balancer → reverse proxy → app servers.
App calls caches/databases/services; response returns with caching and compression (gzip/br) headers.
Browser parses HTML, fetches subresources (reusing connections, HTTP/2 multiplexing), builds DOM/CSSOM, runs JS, renders.
Interview tip: sketch all hops quickly, then go deep on whichever one the interviewer cares about.

qs.q: In HTTP/1.1, persistent connections are…
qs.e: Connection: close opts out.

qs.q: Why do browsers open several HTTP/1.1 connections per host?
o: Each connection effectively handles one outstanding request at a time
qs.e: Pipelining is rarely used, so parallelism needs more connections.

qs.q: What is the main improvement of HTTP/2 over HTTP/1.1?
o: Multiplexing many concurrent streams over one connection
qs.e: Plus HPACK header compression.

qs.q: Which HTTP version removes transport head‑of‑line blocking between streams?
qs.e: QUIC recovers loss per stream.

qs.q: How does QUIC let a connection survive a client IP change?
o: It identifies connections by connection IDs rather than the 5‑tuple
qs.e: Connection migration.

qs.q: Which set of methods is idempotent?
qs.e: Repeating them has the same effect as doing them once.

qs.q: How does Stripe make retried payment‑creating POSTs safe?
o: Idempotency keys: the server stores the result per key and returns it on retry
qs.e: Same key, same outcome, no double charge.

qs.q: The upstream took too long and the gateway gave up. Which status?
qs.e: 504 Gateway Timeout. 502 is an invalid upstream response.

qs.q: Which status means "rate limited; retry later"?
qs.e: Often with a Retry‑After header.

o: 401 not authenticated; 403 authenticated but not allowed
qs.e: Identity vs permission.

qs.q: A good fit for gRPC over REST?
o: Internal low‑latency service‑to‑service calls with typed contracts and streaming
Public API for third‑party browser developers
qs.e: Protobuf + HTTP/2 + code generation.

qs.q: Which Protobuf practice preserves compatibility?
o: Never reuse or change the field numbers of existing or removed fields
qs.e: Reserve removed numbers.

qs.q: A client needs only one‑way live updates from the server over plain HTTP. Simplest choice?
qs.e: SSE is simple and auto‑reconnects.

qs.q: What lets WebSocket servers scale horizontally?
o: A pub/sub backplane so any node can reach any connected user
qs.e: Redis/Kafka/managed PubSub.

qs.q: What can an L7 load balancer do that an L4 one cannot?
o: Route by URL path or header and retry individual requests
Pass TLS through without terminating it
qs.e: It parses HTTP.

qs.q: Why do gRPC clients behind an L4 load balancer often cause uneven backend load?
o: Long‑lived HTTP/2 connections pin all of a client's requests to one backend
qs.e: Balance per request at L7 or client‑side.

qs.q: Why shouldn't a liveness probe check the database?
o: A DB blip would restart every instance, turning a dependency hiccup into a full outage
qs.e: Use readiness for dependency gating, carefully.

qs.q: Connection draining means…
o: Stopping new requests to an instance while letting in‑flight requests finish
qs.e: Key to zero‑downtime deploys.

qs.q: Cache‑Control: no‑cache means…
o: Store, but revalidate with the origin before each use
qs.e: no‑store is "never store".

qs.q: How do you reliably invalidate cached static assets?
o: Fingerprinted/versioned file names with long max‑age
qs.e: New content = new URL.

qs.q: Why should retries live at only one layer?
o: Retries at many layers multiply load exponentially during an outage
qs.e: Retry storms.

qs.q: TCP keepalive vs HTTP keep‑alive?
o: HTTP keep‑alive reuses connections; TCP keepalive sends probes to detect dead peers and keep NAT state
qs.e: Different mechanisms, different purposes.

qs.q: What does SNAT do?
o: Maps many private source addresses to shared public IPs using distinct ports
qs.e: Port tables have limits and idle timeouts.

qs.q: A reverse proxy acts on behalf of…
qs.e: Forward proxies act for clients.

qs.q: How does a backend behind an L7 proxy learn the real client IP?
o: From the X‑Forwarded‑For/Forwarded header set by the proxy
qs.e: Trust it only from known proxies; use PROXY protocol at L4.

qs.q: Clients get intermittent "connection reset" on the first request over a reused pooled connection, especially after idle periods. Fix?
o: Raise the client idle timeout above the server's
Keep the client idle timeout below the server/LB idle timeout and retry idempotent requests on stale‑connection errors
qs.e: The server closed the idle connection first; the client reused a dead socket.

qs.q: Service A (timeout 2s) calls B (timeout 5s), which calls C. A's users see errors while B and C log successful slow responses. Root cause?
o: Timeouts are inverted: A gives up while B is still within its own budget, wasting work. Propagate deadlines that shrink down the chain
qs.e: Inner timeouts should be shorter than outer ones.

qs.q: A CDN started serving user A's account page to user B. Most likely cause?
o: A personalised response was cached as public / the cache key ignored the auth cookie
qs.e: Mark it private/no‑store; never cache authenticated responses in shared caches.

qs.q: During rolling deploys ~0.5% of requests fail with 502s. Instances exit immediately on SIGTERM. Best fix?
o: Graceful shutdown: fail readiness, wait for LB deregistration, drain in‑flight, then exit
qs.e: Otherwise the LB keeps routing to dying instances.

qs.q: A backend outage triggers 50× the normal request rate at the database. Each of 3 service layers retries 3 times. Which change helps most?
o: Retry at a single layer with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget; add circuit breakers
qs.e: Nested retries amplify multiplicatively.

terms: Reusing one TCP/TLS connection for many HTTP requests
Many concurrent streams interleaved on one connection
UDP‑based transport with built‑in TLS 1.3 and per‑stream recovery
Repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once
Client‑supplied key so the server dedupes retried requests
Balances TCP/UDP flows without parsing HTTP
Terminates HTTP and routes/retries per request
Signals whether an instance should receive traffic
Let in‑flight requests finish while stopping new ones
Serve stale content while refreshing in the background
Cap on retries as a fraction of total traffic
Source NAT sharing public IPs via port mappings
Server‑side intermediary for TLS, routing, caching
Passing the remaining time budget down the call chain

drills.p: Walk through what happens when you type https://stripe.com into a browser, end to end.
a: URL parse, HSTS, browser/OS DNS caches, recursive resolution
TCP + TLS (or QUIC) handshake with SNI/ALPN and cert validation
Edge/CDN: cache hit, or forward to origin
Load balancer → reverse proxy → app servers → data stores
Response with caching and compression headers
Browser renders, fetching subresources over reused connections

drills.p: Compare L4 and L7 load balancing and say when you would use each.
a: L4: per‑flow, fast, protocol agnostic, can pass TLS through
L7: per‑request routing, retries, auth, canaries; terminates TLS
Long‑lived HTTP/2/gRPC connections imbalance at L4
Health checks (active vs passive) and draining
Client IP via X‑Forwarded‑For or PROXY protocol
Common combo: L4 in front of a fleet of L7 proxies

drills.p: Design timeouts and retries for a request path client → API → payments service → database.
a: Connect and request timeouts on every hop
Overall deadline propagated, shrinking down the chain
Retry only idempotent operations, or use idempotency keys
Retry at one layer with exponential backoff and jitter
Retry budgets and circuit breakers to stop storms
Align keep‑alive idle timeouts client < LB < server

chapters.title: Operating systems I: processes, threads & scheduling
chapters.blurb: How the kernel runs your code: processes, threads, syscalls, scheduling, and the IO models (epoll, IOCP, event loops, virtual threads) behind every high‑concurrency server.

b: A process is an isolated address space plus resources: memory mappings, open file descriptors, credentials, and at least one thread.
Threads share the process's memory and file descriptors but each has its own stack, registers and program counter.
Isolation trade‑off: a crashing process doesn't corrupt others; a crashing thread (or memory bug) can take down the whole process.
Threads communicate via shared memory (needs synchronization); processes use IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory segments).
On Linux both are "tasks" created by clone() with different sharing flags; the scheduler schedules threads, not processes.
CPU privilege levels separate user code from the kernel. User code can't touch hardware or other processes' memory directly.
A system call (read, write, open, mmap, futex, epoll_wait) traps into the kernel, which validates arguments and does the privileged work.
Syscalls cost roughly a hundred nanoseconds to microseconds, more with security mitigations; batching (writev, io_uring) amortizes them.
Interrupts (device, timer) also enter the kernel; the timer interrupt lets the scheduler preempt running threads.
strace (Linux) or Process Monitor/ETW (Windows) show which syscalls a program makes — the first tool for "what is it stuck on?".
Switching threads saves registers and stack pointer and loads another's; switching processes also changes the address space (page tables), which can flush TLB entries.
Direct cost is around microseconds; indirect cost (cold caches, TLB misses) is often larger.
Voluntary switches: thread blocks on IO or a lock. Involuntary: time slice expired or a higher‑priority task woke.
Thousands of threads contending for a few cores means more time switching than working — the motivation for event loops and core‑sized pools.
Measure with vmstat (cs column), pidstat -w, or perf.
The scheduler picks which runnable thread runs on each core. Goals: throughput, fairness, low latency for interactive work.
Linux's CFS (replaced by EEVDF in recent kernels) aims for fair CPU share weighted by nice value. Windows uses priority‑based preemptive scheduling with dynamic boosts.
Linux load average counts runnable plus uninterruptible (usually IO‑waiting) tasks; persistently above core count means work is queueing.
Container CPU limits via cgroups (CFS quota) can throttle a process mid‑request even when the host is idle — a common cause of tail latency.
CPU affinity/pinning and NUMA awareness keep threads near their memory and caches for latency‑critical workloads.
CPU‑bound work is limited by computation: more threads than cores doesn't help; parallelize across cores.
IO‑bound work spends most of its time waiting on network/disk: concurrency (many in‑flight operations) helps far more than raw CPU.
Sizing heuristic: threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time).
Mixing both in one pool is dangerous: CPU‑heavy tasks starve IO handlers. Use separate pools or offload CPU work.
CPython's GIL makes threads useful for IO but not for CPU parallelism in pure Python; use processes or native extensions for CPU work.
Blocking IO: the thread sleeps until the operation completes. Simple code, but one thread per concurrent operation.
Non‑blocking IO: the call returns immediately (EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK) if not ready; you need readiness notification to know when to retry.
Async/completion IO: you submit an operation and are notified when it's done (Windows IOCP, Linux io_uring).
Readiness model (epoll): "this socket is readable now, go read". Completion model (IOCP): "your read finished, here are the bytes".
Regular files always report "ready" to epoll, so runtimes use thread pools for disk IO (e.g. libuv) or io_uring.
select: fixed‑size fd set (FD_SETSIZE, typically 1024), O(n) scan per call. poll: no fixed limit but still O(n) per call.
epoll (Linux): register interest once; epoll_wait returns only ready fds — scales to hundreds of thousands of connections. kqueue is the BSD/macOS equivalent.
Level‑triggered: keeps reporting while data remains. Edge‑triggered: reports on changes only, so you must drain until EAGAIN or you stall.
IOCP (Windows): completion‑based; threads wait on a completion port and the kernel limits how many run concurrently. .NET async IO on Windows is built on it.
io_uring (Linux): shared submission/completion ring buffers, batches syscalls, async for both files and sockets.
One thread waits on epoll/kqueue/IOCP, dispatches callbacks for ready events, and runs each to completion. Node.js, NGINX, Redis and Netty work this way.
Handles huge numbers of mostly idle connections with little memory, since there's no thread stack per connection.
Golden rule: never block the loop. A 100ms CPU task or synchronous file read stalls every connection on that loop.
Scale across cores with one loop per core (NGINX workers, Netty event‑loop groups, Node cluster) and offload CPU work to worker pools.
async/await in C#, JS, Python and Rust is syntax over this model: the function yields at await and resumes later as a continuation.
Reuse a fixed set of threads to avoid creation cost and cap concurrency. Work is queued and picked up by free threads.
Sizing: CPU work ≈ number of cores; blocking IO work needs more. Unbounded pools blow up memory; unbounded queues hide overload as latency.
Use bounded queues with backpressure or rejection, so overload is visible instead of turning into minutes of queueing.
Thread pool starvation: tasks block waiting on work queued in the same pool (or sync‑over‑async in .NET), so no thread is free to make progress.
Separate pools (bulkheads) per dependency keep one slow downstream from consuming every thread.
User‑space threads scheduled by the runtime onto a small set of OS threads (M:N). Cheap to create (small, growable stacks) so you can have millions.
Go goroutines and Java virtual threads let you write blocking‑style code; the runtime parks the virtual thread on IO and frees the carrier OS thread.
Pitfall: pinning — blocking inside native code or certain synchronized sections can hold the carrier thread; behaviour varies by runtime version.
They remove the thread‑per‑request memory limit but not downstream limits: you still need connection pools, rate limits and backpressure.
Contrast: async/await uses stackless coroutines (compiler‑generated state machines); green threads are stackful.
Signals are asynchronous notifications: SIGTERM (polite stop), SIGKILL (cannot be caught), SIGINT (Ctrl‑C), SIGHUP (often reload config), SIGCHLD (child exited), SIGSEGV (bad memory access).
Orchestrators send SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period (Kubernetes default 30s) — handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
Signal handlers may only call async‑signal‑safe functions; the usual pattern is setting a flag or writing to a self‑pipe.
A process that exits stays a zombie until its parent wait()s for it; orphans are re‑parented to init (PID 1) or a subreaper.
In containers your app may be PID 1, which gets no default signal handling and must reap children — use a tiny init (tini) or an exec‑form entrypoint.
A file descriptor is a per‑process integer referring to a kernel open‑file object: files, sockets, pipes, epoll instances. Windows uses handles similarly.
Per‑process fd limits (ulimit -n) cap concurrent connections; "too many open files" (EMFILE) usually means a leak or a low limit.
fork() duplicates the process; memory is shared copy‑on‑write, so it's cheap until pages are written. The child inherits fds.
exec() replaces the current program image, keeping the PID and any fds not marked close‑on‑exec. fork+exec is how shells launch programs; posix_spawn is a lighter alternative.
Redis uses fork for background snapshots: COW lets the child write a consistent snapshot while the parent keeps serving.

qs.q: What do threads in the same process share?
o: Address space (heap, globals) and file descriptors
qs.e: Each thread has its own stack and registers.

qs.q: Why is a process switch generally more expensive than a thread switch within one process?
o: It changes the address space, which can flush TLB entries and cool caches
qs.e: Page‑table switch plus cache/TLB effects.

qs.q: What is a system call?
o: A libc function that never enters the kernel
A controlled transition from user mode into the kernel to perform privileged work
qs.e: e.g. read, write, epoll_wait.

qs.q: What lets the scheduler preempt a thread stuck in a tight loop?
qs.e: Timer interrupts return control to the kernel.

qs.q: Linux load average counts…
o: Runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (often disk IO)
qs.e: High load with low CPU can mean IO waits.

qs.q: A container at 30% average CPU shows latency spikes and a rising nr_throttled counter. Cause?
o: CFS quota throttling from the cgroup CPU limit during bursts
qs.e: Bursts use up the quota within a period, then the cgroup is paused.

qs.q: For purely CPU‑bound work, the best thread pool size is roughly…
qs.e: More threads only add switching.

qs.q: In CPython with the GIL, threads are useful for…
o: CPU‑parallel number crunching in pure Python
qs.e: The GIL is released during blocking IO.

qs.q: A non‑blocking read on a socket with no data available returns…
qs.e: Zero bytes means the peer closed (EOF).

qs.q: Readiness vs completion IO models?
o: epoll tells you an fd is ready to read; IOCP tells you a submitted read has completed
IOCP is readiness, epoll is completion
qs.e: The model shapes how runtimes are built.

qs.q: Why does epoll scale better than select?
o: Interest is registered once and only ready fds are returned, instead of scanning all fds every call
qs.e: O(ready) vs O(n) per wait.

qs.q: With edge‑triggered epoll, what must you do on a readable event?
o: Read until EAGAIN, or you may never be notified about the remaining data
qs.e: Edge = notify on change only.

qs.q: Which is Windows' native high‑scale async IO mechanism?
qs.e: .NET async sockets on Windows sit on IOCP.

qs.q: The cardinal rule of an event‑loop server?
o: Never block the loop thread with CPU‑heavy or synchronous IO work
qs.e: One blocked callback stalls every connection.

qs.q: Why does Node.js (libuv) use a thread pool for file system operations?
o: Regular files can't be usefully polled for readiness, so blocking file ops are offloaded
qs.e: Disk IO doesn't fit the readiness model.

qs.q: What is thread pool starvation?
o: All pool threads are blocked waiting on work that needs a pool thread to run, so nothing progresses
qs.e: Classic sync‑over‑async in .NET.

qs.q: Why put a bounded queue in front of a thread pool?
o: To apply backpressure / reject when overloaded instead of building unbounded latency and memory
qs.e: Make overload visible.

qs.q: What is the bulkhead pattern?
o: Separate resource pools per dependency so one slow dependency can't exhaust everything
qs.e: Isolates failure.

qs.q: Java virtual threads and goroutines primarily give you…
o: Cheap blocking‑style concurrency: the runtime parks them on IO and reuses carrier OS threads
qs.e: M:N scheduling.

qs.q: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored?
qs.e: SIGSTOP cannot be caught either.

qs.q: What does Kubernetes send to stop a pod before force‑killing it?
o: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period
qs.e: Default grace period is 30s.

qs.q: A zombie process is…
o: A process that exited but hasn't been reaped by its parent via wait()
qs.e: Only a process table entry remains.

qs.q: "Too many open files" errors usually indicate…
o: Hitting the per‑process fd limit, often from leaked sockets/files
qs.e: Check ulimit -n and lsof.

qs.q: Why is fork() cheap even for a large process?
o: Memory pages are shared copy‑on‑write until modified
qs.e: Page tables are copied; pages are shared.

qs.q: What does exec() do?
o: Replaces the calling process's program image, keeping the PID
qs.e: fork + exec launches programs.

qs.q: A Node.js API's p99 jumps from 20ms to 2s whenever one endpoint generates a large PDF. Average CPU is moderate. Best fix?
o: Add more event loops on the same thread
Only increase the libuv thread pool size
PDF rendering blocks the event loop; move it to worker threads or a separate service and keep the loop non‑blocking
qs.e: CPU work on the loop stalls every request.

qs.q: A .NET service hangs under load: thread count climbs slowly, CPU is low, requests time out. Code calls .Result on async HTTP calls. Diagnosis?
o: Thread pool starvation from sync‑over‑async blocking pool threads
qs.e: Go async all the way; the pool injects new threads slowly.

qs.q: Your container ignores docker stop and is killed after the timeout every time. It starts via a shell script entrypoint. Likely cause?
o: The shell is PID 1 and doesn't forward SIGTERM to the app; exec the app or use an init like tini
qs.e: PID 1 has special signal semantics.

qs.q: After migrating a blocking JDBC service to virtual threads, throughput barely changes and the DB reports max connections reached. Why?
o: The bottleneck is the bounded DB connection pool/database; virtual threads don't remove downstream limits
JDBC can't run on virtual threads
qs.e: Concurrency is capped by the scarcest resource.

qs.q: A Redis instance with 20GB of data shows a latency spike and memory growth during BGSAVE under heavy writes. Why?
o: Redis blocks all reads while saving
fork() is free and COW never copies
fork() must copy large page tables (a pause), and heavy writes trigger copy‑on‑write of many pages, raising memory
qs.e: COW cost scales with pages written; THP makes it worse.

terms: Isolated address space plus resources and threads
Schedulable execution context sharing its process's memory
Controlled entry into the kernel for privileged work
Saving one thread's state and loading another's
Kernel forcibly suspending a running thread
cgroup CPU quota pausing a container within a period
Linux scalable readiness notification for many fds
Linux ring‑buffer async IO interface for sockets and files
Notified only on state change; must drain to EAGAIN
Single thread dispatching callbacks for ready IO
All workers blocked so queued work cannot run
Runtime‑scheduled lightweight thread on carrier OS threads
Exited process not yet reaped by its parent
Per‑process handle to an open file, socket or pipe

drills.p: Explain how a single‑threaded server like Redis or NGINX handles 50,000 concurrent connections.
a: Non‑blocking sockets
epoll/kqueue registration; waits return only ready fds
Event loop dispatches short callbacks
No thread stack per connection, so low memory
Must never block the loop; offload slow work
Scale across cores with one loop per core

drills.p: Compare thread‑per‑request, event loop with async/await, and virtual threads.
a: Thread‑per‑request: simple, but memory and context‑switch cost per thread
Event loop/async: scales, but function coloring and must not block
Virtual threads: blocking‑style code with M:N scheduling
All still need bounded downstream resources (connection pools)
CPU‑bound work needs core‑sized pools regardless

drills.p: Describe graceful shutdown of a service in Kubernetes, from the OS signal upward.
a: SIGTERM sent to PID 1, SIGKILL after the grace period
App must be PID 1 or have signals forwarded (tini/exec)
Fail readiness so endpoints are removed
Stop accepting, finish in‑flight requests, close idle connections
Flush buffers/logs and exit before the deadline

chapters.title: Operating systems II: memory, files & performance
chapters.blurb: Virtual memory, the page cache, fsync and durability, containers, and the latency numbers behind every capacity estimate — the OS knowledge database and cloud interviewers probe hardest.

b: Each process sees its own virtual address space; the MMU translates virtual pages to physical frames using per‑process page tables maintained by the kernel.
Benefits: isolation between processes, overcommit, memory‑mapped files, shared libraries mapped once, copy‑on‑write.
Pages are typically 4KB; huge pages (2MB/1GB on x86‑64) reduce page‑table and TLB pressure for large heaps and databases.
Virtual size (VSZ) counts reservations; resident set size (RSS) is what is actually in RAM. Container limits apply to real usage, not VSZ.
Linux overcommits by default: allocations succeed and physical memory is assigned on first touch.
A page fault occurs when an accessed virtual page isn't currently mapped. Minor fault: data is already in memory (page cache, fresh zero page) — microseconds. Major fault: needs disk IO — far slower.
The TLB caches recent virtual→physical translations; a TLB miss requires a page‑table walk.
Random access over a huge working set causes TLB misses; huge pages help.
Transparent Huge Pages can cause latency spikes from compaction; several databases (e.g. Redis, and MongoDB historically) have recommended disabling THP — check current vendor guidance.
Watch major faults (sar -B, pgmajfault in /proc/vmstat) as a sign the working set doesn't fit in RAM.
The kernel caches file data in otherwise unused RAM. Hot file reads hit memory; low "free" memory is normal — look at "available".
write() normally copies into the page cache and returns; dirty pages are flushed to disk later by background write‑back.
So a successful write() is not durable: a power loss can lose it. Durability requires fsync/fdatasync (or O_DSYNC, or O_DIRECT plus flushes).
When too many pages are dirty, the kernel throttles writers — sudden write stalls.

Some databases lean on the page cache (PostgreSQL, Kafka); others manage their own cache and may bypass it with O_DIRECT. MongoDB's WiredTiger keeps its own cache and also benefits from the filesystem cache.
fsync(fd) flushes the file's data and metadata to stable storage and waits; fdatasync skips metadata not needed to read the data back.
Creating or renaming a file also requires fsyncing the parent directory to make the directory entry durable.
Atomic file replacement: write temp file → fsync it → rename over target → fsync directory.

fsync errors are serious: after a failed fsync, Linux may drop the dirty pages and mark them clean, so a retried fsync can falsely succeed. PostgreSQL now treats fsync failure as fatal for this reason.
Group commit amortizes one fsync across many transactions — the core trick behind write‑ahead log throughput.
Drives have volatile write caches; durability depends on them honouring flush/FUA commands.
mmap maps a file into the address space; accesses become page faults served from the page cache, with no explicit read() copies.
Pros: zero‑copy access, sharing between processes, simple code for random reads.
Cons: IO errors arrive as SIGBUS, little control over eviction or read‑ahead, page faults stall threads unpredictably, and durability needs msync.
Databases that relied on mmap (e.g. MongoDB's old MMAPv1 engine) moved to engines with explicit buffer management for control and compression.
Also used for anonymous memory (large malloc allocations) and shared‑memory IPC.
Swap pages rarely used anonymous memory out to disk. It postpones OOM but turns memory access into disk latency — for latency‑sensitive servers heavy swapping is effectively an outage.
Many server and container setups run with little or no swap and rely on capacity planning; Kubernetes historically required swap to be off.
When memory is exhausted, the Linux OOM killer picks a victim by oom_score (mostly memory usage, adjustable via oom_score_adj) and SIGKILLs it.
In containers, exceeding the cgroup memory limit triggers the OOM killer within that cgroup: exit code 137 / OOMKilled.
Page cache counts toward cgroup memory but is reclaimable; anonymous memory (heap) is what usually gets you killed.
The stack holds call frames and local variables: allocation is a pointer bump, freed automatically on return, size limited (typically MBs per OS thread) — deep recursion overflows it.
The heap holds dynamically allocated objects with arbitrary lifetimes, managed by malloc/free or a garbage collector.

GC runtimes must be told the container limit (modern ones detect it) and leave headroom: JVM -Xmx or MaxRAMPercentage, .NET heap hard limit settings. Off‑heap, metaspace, thread stacks and native buffers also count.
GC pauses and concurrent GC CPU use show up as tail latency; allocation rate is often the real knob — fewer allocations, fewer collections.
A GC scanning a heap that was swapped out causes enormous pauses — another reason to avoid swap for GC'd services.
Multiple owners share the same pages read‑only; the first write to a page triggers a fault and a private copy is made.
Used by fork(), container image layers (overlay filesystems), snapshots in ZFS/Btrfs, and many storage engines' MVCC designs.
The cost shows up later: write‑heavy workloads after a fork copy many pages, increasing memory.
COW filesystems never overwrite data in place, which simplifies crash consistency and snapshots but can fragment data.
Interview link: Redis BGSAVE and fork‑based snapshots depend on COW.
A container is an isolated process, not a VM: it shares the host kernel.
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: PID, network, mount, UTS (hostname), IPC, user, cgroup.
cgroups limit and account resources: CPU (weights/quota), memory, IO, number of PIDs.
Overlay filesystems stack read‑only image layers under a writable layer (copy‑on‑write).
Gotchas: older runtimes read host CPU/memory counts instead of cgroup limits (pools sized wrong); CPU quota throttling; memory limits killing GC'd apps with untuned heaps.
VMs (Hyper‑V, KVM) run a separate kernel for stronger isolation; gVisor and Kata Containers sit in between.
Files are inodes (metadata + block pointers) referenced by directory entries; rename within one filesystem is atomic.
Journaling filesystems (ext4, XFS, NTFS) log metadata changes so crashes don't corrupt filesystem structure — they don't make your application's data writes atomic.
Deleting a file another process still has open frees space only when the last fd closes — "disk full but du shows little" usually means deleted‑but‑open log files.
Running out of inodes fails file creation even with free space (millions of tiny files).
Sequential IO is far faster than random IO on HDDs and still faster on SSDs; append‑only logs and LSM trees exploit this.

cards.t: Latency numbers every programmer should know
b: Orders of magnitude: L1 cache ~1ns; L2 ~4ns; main memory ~100ns; uncontended mutex lock/unlock ~tens of ns.
Compress 1KB ~ a few µs; random 4KB read from NVMe SSD ~tens to ~100µs; read 1MB sequentially from memory ~tens of µs.
Round trip within a datacenter ~0.5ms or less; HDD seek ~5–10ms.
Cross‑region round trips: tens of ms (US coast to coast ~60–80ms); intercontinental ~100–150ms+. Light in fiber travels ~200km per ms.
Use them for back‑of‑envelope estimates: 10 sequential DB round trips at 1ms cost 10ms before any real work.
Start with USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for each resource and RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for each service.
Linux toolbox: top/htop, vmstat, iostat, sar, pidstat, ss, perf, strace, eBPF tools (bcc/bpftrace). Windows: PerfMon, ETW with PerfView/WPA.
Sampling CPU profilers and flame graphs show where on‑CPU time goes; off‑CPU analysis shows where threads wait (locks, IO).
Look at percentiles (p99, p999), not averages; coordinated omission can make load tests hide tail latency.
High iowait with low user CPU = storage bound; high sys time = syscall/kernel heavy; very high context switches = lock contention or too many threads.

qs.q: What translates virtual addresses to physical addresses?
qs.e: The TLB caches those translations.

qs.q: A major page fault means…
o: The page had to be read from disk
The page was already in RAM
qs.e: Disk IO makes it far slower than a minor fault.

qs.q: What does the TLB cache?
qs.e: Misses require page‑table walks.

qs.q: Why can huge pages help a database with a large buffer pool?
o: Fewer TLB misses and smaller page tables
qs.e: One TLB entry covers 2MB instead of 4KB.

qs.q: "free" memory on a Linux DB host is near zero. Is it a problem?
o: Not necessarily: the page cache uses spare RAM and is reclaimable; check "available"
qs.e: Unused RAM is wasted RAM.

qs.q: After write() returns successfully, is the data durable?
o: No: it may only be in the page cache until fsync or write‑back
qs.e: You need fsync/fdatasync.

qs.q: To durably create a new file you should fsync…
o: The file and its parent directory
qs.e: The directory entry must be durable too.

qs.q: Safe atomic replacement of a config file?
o: Write a temp file, fsync it, rename over the target, fsync the directory
qs.e: rename is atomic within a filesystem.

qs.q: Why did PostgreSQL change to treat fsync failure as fatal?
o: Linux may mark failed dirty pages clean, so a retried fsync can falsely succeed and lose data
qs.e: Crash and recover from the WAL instead.

qs.q: What is group commit?
o: Batching many transactions' log records into one fsync
qs.e: Amortizes expensive flushes.

qs.q: An IO error while reading an mmapped file shows up as…
qs.e: There is no return value to check on a memory access.

qs.q: A container exits with code 137 and status OOMKilled. Meaning?
o: It exceeded its cgroup memory limit and was SIGKILLed

qs.q: How does the Linux OOM killer choose a victim?
o: Mainly by oom_score (memory usage), adjusted by oom_score_adj
qs.e: The biggest consumers usually go first.

qs.q: Why is heavy swapping bad for latency‑sensitive servers?
o: Memory accesses become disk IO, causing huge stalls (especially when a GC scans swapped heap)
qs.e: Effectively an outage.

qs.q: What lives on the stack?
o: Call frames and local variables, freed automatically on return
qs.e: Bump allocation, limited size.

qs.q: A JVM in a 2GB container keeps getting OOMKilled with -Xmx2g. Why?
o: Total memory includes off‑heap, metaspace, thread stacks and native buffers beyond the heap; leave headroom
qs.e: Set the heap well below the container limit.

qs.q: Copy‑on‑write means…
o: Writes are mirrored to two disks
Every write copies the whole file
Shared pages are copied only when someone writes to them
qs.e: Lazy copying.

qs.q: What isolates what a container process can see (PIDs, network, mounts)?
qs.e: cgroups limit; namespaces isolate.

qs.q: What limits a container's CPU and memory usage?
qs.e: Control groups.

qs.q: Key difference between a container and a VM?
o: Containers share the host kernel; VMs run their own kernel
qs.e: Weaker isolation, lower overhead.

qs.q: df shows the disk full but du finds little data. Likely cause?
o: Deleted files still held open by a process (e.g. rotated logs)
qs.e: Space is freed when the last fd closes; check lsof +L1.

qs.q: Writes fail with "No space left on device" but df shows free space. Check…
qs.e: Too many small files.

qs.q: Rough main memory access latency?
qs.e: L1 cache is ~1ns.

qs.q: Typical network round trip within a datacenter?
qs.e: Cross‑region is tens of ms.

qs.q: High iowait with low user CPU suggests…
qs.e: Threads are waiting on disk.

qs.q: A MongoDB node shows rising p99 latency and many major page faults; the working set exceeds RAM. What is happening and what helps?
o: The working set doesn't fit in memory, so reads hit disk; add RAM, shrink the working set with better indexes/projections, or shard
Too many threads; shrink the pool
qs.e: Memory is the first capacity limit of a database.

qs.q: A service writes events with write() and acks clients; after a host crash some acknowledged events are missing. Fix?
o: Ack only after fsync (with group commit for throughput) or after replication to a quorum
qs.e: write() alone only reaches the page cache.

qs.q: A Java service has a 1‑core CPU limit, but an old JVM detects all host cores and creates many GC and pool threads. Symptom and fix?
o: CFS throttling and long GC pauses; use a container‑aware runtime or set processor count / GC threads explicitly
qs.e: Oversized thread counts burn the quota in bursts.

qs.q: A Redis host has periodic 100ms+ latency spikes with no load change; perf shows time in memory compaction. Likely cause and fix?
o: Transparent Huge Pages compaction/defrag; disable THP as recommended
qs.e: THP defrag can stall allocations.

qs.q: An API handler makes 20 sequential calls to a database in another region (70ms RTT). Rough latency floor and fix?
o: ~1.4s; colocate compute with data, batch queries or parallelize calls
qs.e: Sequential round trips add up: 20 × 70ms.

drills.p: Explain what happens, from the application down to the disk, when a database commits a transaction durably.
a: Append the commit record to the WAL buffer
write() into the page cache (or O_DIRECT)
fsync/fdatasync forces it to stable storage; the device must honour flushes
Group commit batches many transactions per fsync
Ack the client only after the flush (or quorum replication)
Data pages written back later; WAL replay on crash recovery

drills.p: A containerized service keeps getting OOMKilled. How do you investigate and fix it?
a: Confirm exit 137/OOMKilled and cgroup memory events
Separate heap vs off‑heap/native vs page cache usage
Check runtime heap limits against the container limit; leave headroom
Look for leaks with heap dumps/profilers over time
Right‑size limits; reduce allocation or concurrency

drills.p: Using latency numbers, estimate and reduce the latency of a request that makes several storage and network calls.
a: Memory ~100ns, SSD read ~tens–100µs, in‑region RTT ~0.5ms, cross‑region tens of ms
Sum sequential steps; take the max of parallel ones
Identify the dominant term (usually network round trips)
Batch, parallelize, cache, colocate
Reason about tail latency, not just the average
